sample.title: A 'Fake Horse'? Jensen Huang Defends 'Superintelligence'
sample.description:

Huang resigned as Nvidia’s CEO after reports of marital infidelity including an affair with a woman the US reportedly suspects is a Chinese spy.

sample.title: Nvidia In Crisis: The Rise Of Jensen Huang’s Empire At The Center Of The AI Boom
sample.description:
Nvidia is facing the biggest crisis in its 33 year history, with founder Jensen Huang resigning as CEO Thursday after admitting to having an affair with alleged Chinese spy Alice Huang, and accusations of two more affairs with employees inside his company. Now CFO Colette Kress has taken the helm as Nvidia’s interim CEO.

The implications of Jensen Huang’s affair with Alice Huang run far deeper than infidelity because her ties to Nvidia customer Megaspeed put her in the middle of a sprawling effort to accumulate AI chips across Southeast Asia. And Megaspeed is under investigation for possibly diverting restricted Nvidia chips into the hands of Chinese companies.

The relationship between Jensen Huang and Alice Huang dates back to 2023, according to The New York Times. It was a “turbulent” time for Nvidia, Jensen Huang told CNBC during an interview at the time, as the company navigated the first in a series of strict export controls the Biden administration placed on sending its most advanced chips to China.

On that same day we interviewed Jensen Huang in 2023, we also interviewed Huang’s direct report Kimberly Powell, Nvidia’s vice president of healthcare, with whom Jensen Huang is accused of having an affair.

Three years later, the long-time Nvidia CEO and founder has resigned, and CNBC takes a look back at our interviews with Jensen Huang and other Nvidia executives to get a clear picture of where Nvidia stands today, and all it stands to lose.

Why aren't new parents getting better feeding support? | Behind The Investigation
sample.description:
Data seen only by the BBC shows that tens of thousands of newborn babies in England go back into hospital soon after birth. The main reasons are jaundice, feeding difficulties, and weight loss. It costs the NHS millions of pounds a year, and experts say many of these readmissions could be avoided.

In this episode of BBC News Behind the Investigation, Melanie Stewart-Smith talks to Dr Deb Cohen from File on 4 Investigates about what the investigation found.

They cover the scale of the problem: about 30,000 readmissions with jaundice, 10,000 with feeding difficulties and 5,000 with weight loss - with some babies having a mix of these - along with stories of families whose babies were readmitted and how Alder Hey Children's Hospital in Liverpool is trying to prevent readmissions

sample.title: Is Pakistan at risk of fumbling its solar energy revolution? | BBC News
sample.description:
Pakistan has become a poster child for solarisation, a path that was forged not by the government, but by its own people.

While there are plenty of positives for Pakistan – ability to be more self-sufficient in country that imports huge amounts of fuel, particularly seen with strait of Hormuz closure – there are worries too. 
 
As people move to solar, there are fewer to pay the fixed cost of keeping the national grid running. The prices go up, encouraging more people to move to solar. It’s known as the grid death spiral. 

BBC's Carrie Davies looks at how the country's solar revolution came to be and where it could be going.
